outline_section.section_title: Computing Energy of a Finite-Duration Signal from a Graph
outline_section.learning_goal: Read a finite-duration signal from its graph, translate the visible support and segments into integrals, and compute the energy from the plotted shape.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean graph of a finite-duration signal on Cartesian axes: zero outside a compact interval, with a simple triangular or trapezoidal pulse on the support and labeled breakpoints and amplitudes.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a minimal black-and-white math graph with clear numeric labels. The worked example and follow-up questions should use graph data only; the practice graphs should vary the support endpoints and heights while staying simple enough to integrate by hand.

question_policy.answer_format: Five numeric answer choices; the graph supplies the signal shape and the student chooses the correct total energy.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the energy of a different finite-duration signal shown only by a graph, with similarly simple piecewise-linear segments and compact support.
distractor_plan: Read the graph's height or breakpoints incorrectly.
Compute area under the graph instead of energy.
Square only one side of the graph and forget the other segment.
Use the wrong support interval or miss an endpoint.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the energy of the finite-duration signal shown in the graph: a triangular pulse that is zero outside $0 \le t \le 2$, rises linearly from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$, and falls linearly back to $(2,0)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Translate the graph into two linear pieces, square each piece, integrate over $[0,1]$ and $[1,2]$, and add the results to get the total energy.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The signal is now given visually, so the first job is to read support, breakpoints, and heights from the graph before applying the same support-limited energy procedure.
solution_step_plan: Read the support endpoints and the key vertex values directly from the graph.
Write the signal as piecewise formulas on each linear segment.
Square each segment and integrate over its own subinterval.
Add the subinterval energies and simplify the numeric result.
practice_variation_axes: Change the support width or shift the graph along the time axis.
Use a graph with a different piecewise-linear shape but the same overall finite-duration setup.
Vary the number of linear segments while keeping the graph simple enough for hand integration.

outline_section.handoff_notes: This is the only image-driven section in the lesson. The graph should be the problem data, not decoration, and the follow-up questions should reuse the same skill with new graph images.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the energy of the finite-duration signal shown in the graph?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the support from the graph: the signal is nonzero only on $0 \le t \le 2$. On $0 \le t \le 1$, the line is $x(t)=t$; on $1 \le t \le 2$, the line is $x(t)=2-t$.
Each side contributes $\frac{1}{3}$, so the total energy is $\frac{2}{3}$. The area under the graph is not the answer; the signal must be squared before integrating.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the energy of the finite-duration signal shown in the graph?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the support from the graph: the signal is nonzero only on $-1 \le t \le 3$. On $-1 \le t \le 1$, the rising segment is $x(t)=t+1$; on $1 \le t \le 3$, the falling segment is $x(t)=3-t$.
Each half contributes $\frac{8}{3}$, so the total energy is $\frac{16}{3}$. Using the graph's area alone would give $4$, which is the wrong quantity.
